question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The variance explained by a polygenic score is necessarily lower than SNP heritability because real-world PGS construction is constrained by finite discovery-sample sizes, imperfect LD tagging of causal variants, and residual population stratification that cannot be fully eliminated. Even with large biobanks and sophisticated methods such as LDpred or PRS-CS, the realized R² falls short of the SNP-heritability ceiling obtained from GREML or LD-score regression on the same data; regularization and shrinkage further guarantee that equality is never attained.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True
The SNP heritability represents an upper bound on the additive genetic variance tagged by common variants, but a polygenic score is constructed from finite samples with imperfect LD tagging, residual stratification, and regularization that shrinks effect sizes. These factors ensure the out-of-sample R² of even the best PGS will fall short of the SNP-h² estimate, at least in any realistic dataset. In principle an arbitrarily large, perfectly homogeneous sample might close the gap, yet the practical ceiling remains strictly lower.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability of a phenotype represents the total proportion of variance that can be explained by SNPs (an upper bound given the data). A polygenic score constructed from those SNPs can, in the theoretical limit of infinite sample size and perfect effect-size estimation, recover essentially all of that variance; its out-of-sample R² is therefore bounded above by, but not necessarily strictly below, SNP heritability. In practice the achieved R² is lower, yet the word “necessarily” makes the claim false.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance that would be captured if every SNP’s true (population) effect size were known exactly. A polygenic score, by contrast, is constructed from estimated effect sizes obtained in a finite discovery sample. Because those estimates contain sampling error, shrinkage, imperfect LD tagging, and possible stratification artifacts, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any PGS is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) for any finite discovery sample. Only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly representative data would the two quantities coincide; hence the predictive ability “is necessarily lower.”

(The statement is therefore true.)

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance that is in principle linearly explained by the additive effects of all measured (or imputed) SNPs. A polygenic score (PGS) is simply a linear predictor formed from a finite set of estimated SNP effect sizes. In the theoretical limit of infinite GWAS sample size, perfect linkage-disequilibrium information, and an exhaustive set of SNPs, the PGS recovers exactly those SNP effects; its out-of-sample \(R^2\) therefore converges to \(h^2_{SNP}\). Consequently the inequality “PGS \(R^2 < h^2_{SNP}\)” is not strictly necessary—it is an empirical consequence of finite data and imperfect estimation, not a mathematical requirement. The PGS \(R^2\) cannot exceed \(h^2_{SNP}\), but equality is attainable under idealized conditions; hence the claim is false.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

SNP heritability represents the theoretical maximum proportion of phenotypic variance that can be captured by additive SNP effects (i.e., the upper bound on out-of-sample prediction R²). With infinite GWAS sample size and perfect effect-size estimates (or equivalently, with a method that recovers the exact SNP effects), a polygenic score can in principle attain this bound; therefore the predictive R² is not necessarily strictly lower than SNP heritability. In finite samples the R² is lower due to estimation error, but the statement claims necessity, which does not hold.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the total fraction of phenotypic variance that is additively explained by the set of SNPs (i.e., \(\mathrm{Var}(X\beta)/\mathrm{Var}(Y)\)). Any polygenic score is a linear predictor \(\hat{G}=X\hat{\beta}\) whose weights \(\hat{\beta}\) are estimated from finite data; the estimation error in \(\hat{\beta}\) (plus any additional loss from LD pruning, shrinkage, or imperfect tagging) guarantees that \(R^2(Y,\hat{G})<h^2_{SNP}\) in any real sample. Only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained data would equality be reached; under all practical conditions the inequality is therefore strict.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability of a phenotype represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is tagged by (and thus predictable from) the SNPs in aggregate. A polygenic score (PGS) is simply a linear combination of those same SNPs; with sufficiently large discovery samples the estimated SNP weights converge to their true values, so the out-of-sample R² of the PGS can asymptotically reach (but need not fall short of) the SNP heritability. The statement therefore claims a strict inequality that does not necessarily hold.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability represents the total phenotypic variance that can be explained by the optimal linear combination of all SNPs (i.e., the population-level best linear predictor). A polygenic score is simply an empirical estimate of that same linear predictor. With infinite training-sample size the estimated weights converge to the true weights, so the out-of-sample R² converges to the SNP heritability; equality is therefore attainable in the theoretical limit. The statement’s use of “necessarily” is therefore incorrect.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP-based heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the best linear predictor that uses all SNPs (i.e., the squared correlation between phenotype and the optimal linear combination of SNP dosages). A polygenic score is simply one particular linear combination of SNPs. When the weights of that combination converge to the true population coefficients (infinite GWAS sample size, perfect LD coverage, no stratification, etc.), the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of the score equals \(h^2_{SNP}\). Therefore the inequality is not strict; equality is attainable in the theoretical limit, so the claim that predictive ability is “necessarily lower” is false. In finite samples the achieved \(R^2\) will of course fall short, but necessity does not hold.
